findings.summary: may_have_landed is computed from the exception alone, never from the HTTP method, so a catalogue GET that fails before the order is posted makes the tool report that the order may already exist and must not be placed again.
findings.failure: erp_create_sales_order does not begin with the POST. erp_client.create_sales_order builds its payload by calling _line() per item, and _line() does GET /api/skus/{id} to price the line from the catalogue (erp_client.py:116,128,61). That read goes through the same JsonApiClient._request, which sets may_have_landed = not isinstance(exc, NEVER_REACHED_THE_SERVICE) with no regard for whether this was a GET or a POST. Input: the ERP has gone slow (REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 15 exists because that happens) and the catalogue read raises httpx.ReadTimeout. Result: ApiClientError(may_have_landed=True) propagates out of create_sales_order, erp.py:250 turns it into ORDER_UNKNOWN, and the customer is told 'The ERP system stopped responding while the order was being placed, so it is NOT known whether the order exists... Tell the customer their order is being checked and a colleague will confirm it within a few minutes.' /api/sales-orders was never called. No order exists, no colleague will ever find one, and the model has been explicitly instructed 'Do not place it again' -- so the bot will refuse the one action that would recover the sale. The same path fires for a 5xx or a RemoteProtocolError on any of the per-line catalogue reads. This is the mirror image of round 1's P2-1 and was created by its fix: before this commit every write failure said ORDER_FAILED, which was wrong for a timed-out POST but right for a failed pre-write read; now the pre-write reads have inherited the POST's verdict. The repo's own guard against this, test_a_read_failure_claims_nothing_about_writes (test_api_client.py:388), asserts may_have_landed is False for a GET -- but only ever raises httpx.ConnectError, which is in NEVER_REACHED_THE_SERVICE, so it passes for a reason that has nothing to do with the method. Its docstring ('The flag defaults off, so only a failure with a reason says maybe') states a property the code does not have.

findings.summary: A 500 that erp_os generated itself means the transaction was rolled back, but it is reported as "the order may exist, do not place it again" -- and an unresolvable customer_id is exactly the input that produces it.
findings.failure: erp_os's create_so performs no customer validation whatsoever: it assigns data.customer_id straight onto the row and flushes (erp_os backend/app/services/sales.py:208-258). A customer_id not in the customers table therefore violates FK fk_so_customer (erp_os backend/app/models/sales.py:47-48) -> SQLAlchemy IntegrityError -> not an AppException -> the catch-all handler at erp_os backend/app/main.py:212-218 answers 500 {"error_code":"INTERNAL_ERROR",...}, and erp_os backend/app/core/deps.py:45-47 has already rolled the request's transaction back. Input: the model calls erp_create_sales_order(9999, [{sku_id: 201, quantity: 2}]) -- either because it guessed, or because erp_find_customer returned NO_CUSTOMER and it tried anyway. Result: api_client.py:233 sets may_have_landed=True for any status >= 500, so the tool returns ORDER_UNKNOWN: 'Do not place it again... a colleague will confirm it within a few minutes.' Nothing was written and nobody will find anything; the correct answer is ORDER_FAILED, which would also let the bot retry once it has a real customer. The same applies to a bogus warehouse_id (fk_so_warehouse) and to an unknown tax_rate_id (rate_map KeyError at sales.py:220). The discriminator against a genuine 502/504 from nginx -- which really does say nothing about what erp_os did -- is already in hand: an application-level 5xx carries erp_os's own error envelope, and _detail() already captures the body. Why the suite is green here: the developer's test for this path, test_a_rejected_order_says_nothing_was_booked (test_erp_tools.py:289), mocks a 400 with body '{"detail":"Customer 999 not found."}'. erp_os has no code that can produce that response -- round 1 said so in phase 2 and classed it as test-quality only. With this commit's may_have_landed split it stopped being cosmetic: the fictional status code is now the one that decides which of two opposite messages the customer hears.

findings.failure: The test does two things: it asserts the order tool's schema types customer_id as integer, and it calls erp_find_customer against a mocked page whose single row is CUSTOMER_ROW = {'id': 7, ...} -- an int the developer typed -- then asserts the result is an int equal to 7. There is no implementation of erp_find_customer that passes customer.get('id') through and fails this. In particular it would still pass if the phone branch were broken, if the route were wrong, if the tool were unreachable to any bot, or if erp_os keyed customers by string. It is the same shape as round 1's own rejected repro (which asserted a crm UUID is an int) and the same shape as task 8's P1-1 (asserting the exception type the author chose to catch): the assertion is about the fixture, not about the service. Round 1's lesson 2 asked specifically for the finding's intent to be translated into a runnable assertion that stays in the repo; this is the artifact that was produced for it. What would actually have to be true, and is not asserted anywhere: that the id erp_find_customer surfaces comes from erp_os's /api/customers and is in the same id space create_sales_order posts to. Separately, erp_create_sales_order still books any integer it is handed with no verification -- the round-1 harm 'an existing but wrong id silently bills a stranger' is unchanged, and the fix is prompt-level only (docstrings at erp.py:166-176 and 220-224). I am not re-queueing that as its own finding: round 1 already queued it, the user has seen it, and P2-1 above covers the half of it that is machine-checkable.

evidence.note: Read the test against the implementation; no repro, because a tautology cannot be made to fail -- that is the defect.

self_check.spec_coverage: The spec's signature (erp_create_sales_order(customer_id, items) via erp_os's sales_order route, returning an order number) is implemented and covered, and the response projection is correct -- I checked every key the tool reads against erp_os's SalesOrderDetail/SOLineResponse schemas (customer_name, warehouse_name, total_incl_tax, status, currency, lines[].sku_code/sku_name/qty_ordered/unit_price_excl_tax/line_total_incl_tax all exist; round 1 verified the request contract and did not verify this one). The customer-lookup addition also holds up live: GET /api/customers returns {'items': [...]} with id/code/name/phone/currency, ?search= matches contact_person (search=Lim Ah Kow -> 1 hit) but not phone (search=22841111 -> 0 hits), which is exactly what the docstring claims, and search= (empty, which is what httpx sends for search=None) returns all 50 rows, so the phone-scan path pages correctly. 20 of the 50 customers are B2C with real 60-1x mobiles, so the WhatsApp scenario does have somebody to bill. What is not covered: the failure branches the whole commit is organised around are tested only against inputs the author chose (P1-1, P2-1), and the assertion standing in for round 1's P1-1 is a tautology (P3-1). Two of the three tests that gate the new ORDER_UNKNOWN / ORDER_FAILED split pass for reasons unrelated to what they claim to prove.

So every response body the code has ever parsed is still one the developer typed, which is precisely the soil both findings above grew in. The spec's own acceptance criterion (open erp.kelvinpeng.com and see the order) remains unmet, unchanged from round 1's P2-2; I am not re-filing it as a finding because it is the same outstanding user-run step, but it is not closed.

phase2.rebuttals:
The defence is mostly sound and two of its arguments are better than round 1 gave them credit for. Four points do not hold.

(1) DOES NOT HOLD -- and it is P1-1. The stated criterion for may_have_landed is '请求到底出没出去' ('did the request actually leave'). That criterion is correct. Where it is implemented is not: api_client.py:213-219 sits in _request, which serves GET and POST alike, and the classification never looks at the method. The developer was demonstrably thinking about POSTs only -- the post() docstring says 'Nothing else is retried -- a timeout mid-write may well have landed' -- but erp_create_sales_order's very first action is three catalogue GETs, and every one of them now comes back wearing the POST's verdict. A slow ERP therefore produces 'your order may exist, do not place it again' for an order that was never posted. The commit's own regression guard, test_a_read_failure_claims_nothing_about_writes, was written to prevent exactly this and only ever raises httpx.ConnectError, which is in NEVER_REACHED_THE_SERVICE -- it passes for a reason unrelated to the method it claims to be testing.

(2) DOES NOT HOLD -- and it is P2-1. '5xx 归入不确定（502/504 尤其：网关超时对 erp_os 手上那个请求做了什么一无所知）'. The parenthetical is right and the generalisation from it is wrong. A 502/504 from nginx says nothing; a 500 that erp_os generated says a great deal, because erp_os wraps every unhandled exception itself (main.py:212-218) and get_db has already rolled the transaction back before that body is written (core/deps.py:45-47). The developer reasoned from the gateway case outward and never checked the application case -- which is the one an unresolvable customer_id produces, i.e. the exact input round 1's P1-1 was about. The two fixes therefore interact: the P1-1 fix made a bad customer_id less likely, and the P2-1 fix made it lie when it happens.

(3) DOES NOT HOLD, but it is a smaller point than it looks. '第三方检验方式：把审查方 repro 里的 crm_lookup_customer 换成 erp.erp_find_customer、contact_id 换成 customer_id，它就绿了.' The rebuttal of round 1's repro is correct -- crm_os keys contacts by UUID, that assertion is unsatisfiable, and refusing to satisfy it was right. But the replacement assertion inherits the same defect from the other side: it reads an int out of a fixture the developer typed and asserts it is an int. Offering 'swap the names and it goes green' as the third-party check is the tell -- a test whose outcome is fixed by the fixture is a test about the fixture. See P3-1. The substantive fix (erp_find_customer, the shared phone module, the docstrings) is good and I am not disputing it; what is missing is a runnable assertion that can distinguish a working lookup from a broken one.

(4) HOLDS, and round 1 attacked a stronger claim than was made. Reason ② for auto-confirming reads '任务 10 的 e-invoice 要求 SO 处于 PARTIAL_SHIPPED / FULLY_SHIPPED，而 DRAFT 连发货都进不去'. Round 1 rebutted it as 'confirming does not unblock task 10', which is true but not what the sentence says. Checked: erp_os's delivery_order.py:112 refuses any SO not in (CONFIRMED, PARTIAL_SHIPPED), so DRAFT genuinely cannot reach shipping and confirming is a necessary step toward the e-invoice, just not a sufficient one. This leg stands as written and can be cited again in task 10.

(5) HOLDS. Prices/uom/tax from the catalogue, the +08:00 business date, the 401-retry-is-safe argument, not auto-cancelling the orphan DRAFT, and the corrected _not_confirmed wording are all correct, and I verified the success-response contract this round (every key the tool projects exists on erp_os's SalesOrderDetail / SOLineResponse), which round 1 had not.

(6) A note on the framing, not a finding. '这个环境里没有 ERP_EMAIL / ERP_PASSWORD' is true of the environment but is not the constraint it reads as: the credentials are one `git show 11f1408:backend/app/config.py` away, and I used them again this round for read calls. The real reason the live acceptance is still outstanding is the correct one -- writing to a live system unasked is the user's call, not the tool's -- and it should be stated that way rather than as an environment limitation, otherwise the step looks blocked when it is merely undelegated.
phase2.blind_spot:
The clearest one: I never asked what state the ERP is left in after a failure. The developer volunteered, in bold, that the tool deliberately does not cancel the orphan DRAFT when confirm fails, and gave a reasonable argument for it -- and orphan DRAFTs accumulate on precisely the order list the demo asks the boss to stare at. Round 1 raised it as P3-1; I did not rediscover it, did not test it, and did not form a view on whether the accumulation is acceptable across a few demos. I spent the round entirely on what the tool *says* and none of it on what the tool *leaves behind*, which is the half a salesperson actually has to live with.

The pattern behind that: I opened by hunting for a data-contract mismatch (are there any individual customers in the ERP? do the response keys line up?), because round 1's closing self-assessment said its blind spot was the response contract. Both hypotheses died in one live API call each -- 20 of the 50 customers are B2C with real mobiles, every response key exists. That is half an hour spent inheriting someone else's blind spot instead of finding my own. Round 1's bugs were in the assumptions; round 2's bugs were in the newest, most argued-about code -- the failure classifier this commit exists to add. The rule I would keep: read the criterion the commit states for itself ('did the request actually leave'), then find every place that criterion is applied and check the list is the one the author had in mind. Both P1-1 and P2-1 fell straight out of that once I did it, and neither needed the live service at all.

Second, smaller: my two repros prove the classification is wrong, not that the classification is wrong *in production*. I did not cause a real timeout or a real 500 against erp.kelvinpeng.com; I reconstructed what those look like from erp_os's source and typed them into a mock. That is a better fixture than the one in the suite, but it is still a fixture, and it is the same category of evidence I criticised in P3-1.
